title: Medina, the Community and the Occasions of Revelation
bigQuestion: How did the move to Medina change the Muslim community, and how does knowing the occasion of a verse change the way it is read?

story.title: The Verse After the Dispute
story.kicker: In the market of Medina, a buyer and a seller argue over a measure of dates, and the argument becomes the subject of a surah.
paragraphs: It is a morning in the market of Medina, a few years after the Muslims arrived from Mecca. The town is nothing like Mecca. It is an oasis of date palms and small farms, spread out in clusters of houses and forts. Its people are farmers as much as traders. At the market, a woman sets down her basket and asks for a measure of dates. The seller fills the measure, but he fills it lightly and shakes it so the dates settle low. When he buys, tradition says, men like this demand the measure heaped full. When they sell, they give short.

The woman objects. The seller shrugs; this is how it has always been done. A crowd gathers. Some of the Muslims who came from Mecca, the *Muhajirun*, know this kind of trick well; Meccan merchants had done the same. Some of the Medinans who welcomed them, the *Ansar*, are embarrassed. Somebody says they should take the matter to the Prophet. In Medina, unlike Mecca, Muhammad is not only a preacher. He is the man the town's agreement names as judge.

A report preserved in later hadith collections, going back to the Prophet's cousin Ibn Abbas, says that when Muhammad came to Medina, its people were among the worst at giving short measure. Then, the report says, God sent down the opening of Surah 83, Al-Mutaffifin, "The Defrauders." It pronounces woe on those who demand full measure when they buy but give less when they sell, and it asks whether they do not think they will be raised up on a mighty day. After that, the report says, they gave good measure.

Muslim scholars call a report like this an *occasion of revelation*, in Arabic sabab al-nuzul. It tells the situation in which a verse came. Not every verse has one, and scholars often disagree about which report is right. Some say Surah 83 is Meccan, not Medinan. But the idea is the same either way. To read a verse well, it helps to know what it was answering.

That is this chapter's second subject. Its first is the city itself: how a group of refugees became a community with a mosque, an agreement, an army and a calendar, and how, within ten years, they returned to Mecca. Both subjects meet in the market. The community made rules for daily life, and the verses that came in Medina are full of daily life: trade, debt, marriage, food, war and peace.
story.think: If you knew that a verse was first spoken to settle an argument about dates in a market, would you read it differently than if you only had the words? What might you notice, and what might you miss?

lessons.title: The Hijra and the Calendar
lessons.mainIdea: In 622 Muhammad and the Muslims moved from Mecca to Yathrib, later called Medina; Muslims count their calendar from this hijra.
reading: Yathrib was an oasis town about 210 miles north of Mecca. Its Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, had been fighting one another for years, and its Jewish tribes had their own forts and farms. Tradition says some pilgrims from Yathrib met Muhammad in Mecca in 620, and that in 621 and 622 larger groups made pledges to him at a place called Aqaba. They promised to protect him as they would their own families. They wanted a fair judge from outside their feuds. Muhammad, with no protector in Mecca since Abu Talib's death, accepted.

Through the summer of 622 the Muslims left Mecca in small groups. Tradition says Quraysh plotted to kill Muhammad, and that he slipped out with Abu Bakr and hid in a cave on Mount Thawr for three days before reaching Yathrib in September. This move is the *hijra*, from the Arabic for "leaving" or "migration." Those who made it were called the *Muhajirun*, the emigrants. The people of Yathrib who took them in were called the *Ansar*, the helpers. The town itself came to be called Madinat al-Nabi, "the city of the Prophet," or simply Medina.

The hijra is the turning point of Muhammad's story as Muslims tell it. In Mecca, he had been a preacher without power. In Medina, he became the head of a community. When the second caliph, Umar, set up an Islamic calendar around 638, tradition says he chose the year of the hijra, not the year of the first revelation or the Prophet's birth, as year one. Muslim dates are written AH, from the Latin for "in the year of the hijra." The Islamic year follows the moon and is about eleven days shorter than the solar year.

The Qur'an speaks of the emigrants and helpers as two groups God is pleased with (9:100), and it praises those who "left their homes" for God's sake. Later Muslims used hijra as a word for leaving a bad place or a bad way of life for a better one. For a historian, 622 is also the earliest date in Muhammad's life that outside evidence supports fairly well, because the Islamic calendar, and coins dated by it, start there.

words.d: the migration of Muhammad and the Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622; year one of the Islamic calendar
'the emigrants,' the Muslims who left Mecca for Medina
'the helpers,' the people of Medina who took the emigrants in
'in the year of the hijra,' the label for years in the Islamic calendar

check.q: Who were the Ansar?

lessons.title: The Agreement of Medina
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition preserves an agreement between Muhammad, the Muslims and the tribes of Medina, including Jewish tribes, that made them one community for defense.
reading: Soon after the hijra, tradition says, Muhammad drew up a written agreement among the people of Medina. Ibn Ishaq's sira preserves its text. Modern writers call it the *Constitution of Medina*, though it is more like a treaty. It says the believers from Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who join them, form one *ummah*, one community, apart from other people. It sets rules for blood money and ransom, forbids helping an enemy against the community, and says disputes are to be referred to God and to Muhammad.

The agreement also names several Jewish clans of Medina. It says the Jews are a community alongside the believers: the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs. Each side pays its own costs, each helps the other against attack, and neither may go to war without the other's consent. Historians take this document seriously. Its plain, old-fashioned language and its lack of later Islamic terms suggest it is genuinely early, and most think it reflects real arrangements from the first years in Medina.

For the study of the Qur'an, two things stand out. First, the ummah at this point included non-Muslims as partners. The word ummah appears in the Qur'an for the Muslim community and also for other peoples and even for animals (6:38). Second, Muhammad's role changed. In Mecca he had been a messenger only. In Medina he was also a judge and a leader, and the verses of this period reflect that: they address the community about its rules.

Sunni and Shia readers, as well as modern Muslim writers on citizenship, often point to this agreement as a model of a community that includes different faiths under shared rules. Historians caution that it was an arrangement for one small town, and that relations with several of the Jewish clans broke down within a few years, as the next lessons tell. Both points are true, and both matter.

words.d: the modern name for the early agreement, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, among Muhammad, the Muslims and the tribes of Medina
a community; in the Qur'an and the Medina agreement, the community of believers and those joined to it

look.title: One Community, Two Religions
look.text: The agreement, as Ibn Ishaq records it, states that the believers and those who follow them and fight alongside them are one community apart from other people. Of the Jewish clans it says that they are a community alongside the believers; the Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs. It adds that each must help the other against anyone who attacks the people of this document.
look.cite: The agreement of Medina as preserved in Ibn Ishaq's sira (c. 760), in Ibn Hisham's edition, paraphrased
look.prompt: What does the agreement ask each group to share, and what does it let each group keep separate? Why might that arrangement have appealed to a town torn by feuds?

check.q: Where is the text of the agreement of Medina preserved?
check.why: Ibn Ishaq's sira, in Ibn Hisham's edition, records the text; the Qur'an does not contain it.

check.q: What does the agreement say about the Jewish clans it names?
choices: They form a community alongside the believers and keep their own religion
They must pay for the Muslims' wars
check.why: The document says the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs, and that each helps the other against attack.

check.q: Why do most historians think the agreement is genuinely early?
choices: Because it is written in Greek
Because its plain language lacks later Islamic terms
Because it is quoted in the Qur'an
Because it was found on a coin
check.why: Its old-fashioned wording and absence of later technical terms suggest it was not invented afterward.

lessons.title: The Mosque and the Ummah
lessons.mainIdea: In Medina the Muslims built a mosque, paired emigrants with helpers, turned to face Mecca in prayer, and took on the practices that define Muslim life.
reading: Tradition says the first thing Muhammad did in Medina was build a *mosque*. The Arabic word, masjid, means "place of prostration," a place to bow in prayer. The first one was simple: a walled yard of mud brick, palm trunks for pillars, a roof of palm branches over part of it, and rooms along one side where Muhammad's family lived. It was a prayer hall, a meeting place, a court and a school all at once. The Prophet's Mosque in Medina today, vastly enlarged, stands on the same site.

The emigrants had arrived with almost nothing. Tradition says Muhammad paired each Muhajir with an Ansari as a "brother," so the Medinan would share his home and work. This bond of brotherhood, along with the agreement, held the new community together. The Qur'an calls the believers brothers (49:10) and uses the word ummah for the community. Over time ummah came to mean all Muslims everywhere, a meaning it still has.

In Medina the main practices of Islam took their settled form. Tradition says that at first the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem, and that about sixteen months after the hijra a verse (2:144) turned the *qibla*, the direction of prayer, toward the Kaaba in Mecca. Fasting in Ramadan was set (2:183–185). Rules for zakat, the giving to the poor, were laid down. The call to prayer, the adhan, began; Bilal, the freed man from Mecca, gave it. Muslims see these as the Five Pillars taking shape.

Historians note how much this changed the message. In Mecca the Qur'an spoke of belief and judgment. In Medina it also spoke of practice: when to pray, how to fast, what to give. The turn of the qibla from Jerusalem to Mecca, which the Qur'an itself discusses at length, is read by many scholars as a moment when the community defined itself as distinct from the Jews and Christians of Arabia, while still claiming the same God and prophets.

words.d: a Muslim place of prayer; the Arabic masjid means 'place of prostration'
the direction Muslims face in prayer; changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca c. 624 (Qur'an 2:144)
the call to prayer, first given in Medina by Bilal

look.title: A Yard of Palm Trunks
look.text: Picture the first mosque as tradition describes it: a square yard with low mud walls, a row of palm trunks holding up a roof of branches at one end for shade, bare ground, and a few small rooms built into the wall. People pray here, but they also argue cases, hear news, teach children, and sleep when they have nowhere else to go.
look.prompt: What does this building tell you about how the early community saw the line between religious life and everyday life? Compare it with a house of worship you know.

check.q: What does the Arabic word masjid mean?
check.why: Masjid, the word behind 'mosque,' means 'place of prostration,' a place to bow in prayer.

check.q: According to tradition, what did Qur'an 2:144 change?
choices: The direction of prayer, from Jerusalem to Mecca
check.why: The qibla turned from Jerusalem toward the Kaaba about sixteen months after the hijra.

check.q: How did Muhammad help the emigrants who arrived with nothing, according to tradition?
choices: He gave them land in Mecca
He asked the Byzantines for aid
He paired each with a Medinan 'brother' who shared his home and work
check.why: The brotherhood pairing of Muhajirun and Ansar helped hold the new community together.

lessons.title: Badr and Uhud
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition tells of a surprising Muslim victory at Badr in 624 and a costly setback at Uhud in 625; the Qur'an names Badr and reflects on both.
reading: Conflict with Mecca did not end with the hijra. The emigrants had left property behind, and tradition says Muslim raiding parties began to threaten Meccan caravans passing near Medina. In March 624 (Ramadan, 2 AH), a large Meccan force came out to protect a caravan, and the two sides met at wells called *Badr*. The sira reports about 313 Muslims against roughly a thousand Meccans. The Muslims won. Several leaders of Quraysh were killed. The Qur'an names Badr (3:123) and says God helped the believers there when they were weak.

Muslims remember Badr as proof that God was with the small community. The Qur'an's Surah 8, Al-Anfal ("The Spoils of War"), is read by commentators as coming just after the battle. It deals with how to divide what was captured, and it tells the believers that it was God, not they, who won. Historians note that the victory also changed politics in Medina: Muhammad's standing rose, and doubters grew quieter.

A year later, in 625, Mecca struck back. A Meccan army of about three thousand, tradition says, met about seven hundred Muslims at the hill of *Uhud*, just outside Medina. The Muslims held at first, but archers left their post to gather spoils, the Meccan cavalry swung around, and the Muslims were driven back. Muhammad was wounded. His uncle Hamza was killed. The Meccans withdrew without taking the city. Surah 3, Al Imran, discusses the battle at length, blaming disobedience and promising forgiveness (3:152–155).

Told factually, these were two battles between a town and a city over trade, honor and religion, fought by a few thousand men. Their weight in Muslim memory is far larger. Muslims name children after the fighters of Badr, and the lessons of Uhud, obedience and steadiness, are taught to this day. The Qur'an does not describe the fighting in detail. It reflects on what the fighting meant, and that is how its readers have used it.

words.d: the wells where, in 624, a small Muslim force defeated a larger Meccan army; named in Qur'an 3:123
the hill outside Medina where the Meccans defeated the Muslims in 625; discussed in Surah 3
'The Spoils of War,' Surah 8, which commentators read as coming after Badr

check.q: Which verse of the Qur'an names the battle of Badr?
check.why: Qur'an 3:123 names Badr and says God helped the believers when they were weak.

check.q: What happened at Uhud in 625, according to tradition?
choices: The Muslims were driven back after archers left their post

check.q: What does Surah 8, Al-Anfal, mainly deal with?
choices: The spoils of war and the meaning of the victory at Badr

lessons.title: The Trench and the Jewish Tribes
lessons.mainIdea: In 627 Medina withstood a siege at the Trench; in these years relations with three Jewish tribes of Medina broke down, ending in expulsion and, for one tribe, execution.
reading: In 627, tradition says, Quraysh gathered a large alliance of tribes, perhaps ten thousand men, to finish Medina. A Persian companion named Salman suggested digging a trench across the open side of the town, a tactic unknown in Arabia. The attackers could not cross it. After weeks of siege, cold weather and quarrels among the allies, they went home. Surah 33, Al-Ahzab ("The Allies" or "The Confederates"), is read by commentators as speaking of this siege. Muslims call it the Battle of the *Trench*, al-Khandaq.

The years between Badr and the Trench also saw the breakdown of relations with three Jewish tribes of Medina. Told briefly and factually, as the sira tells it: after Badr in 624, a dispute in the market led to the siege and expulsion of the *Banu Qaynuqa*. In 625, after Muhammad accused the *Banu Nadir* of plotting against his life, they were besieged and expelled; Surah 59, Al-Hashr, is read as referring to this. Both tribes left with their movable goods, and many settled at the oasis of Khaybar.

The third case was the harshest. During the Trench, tradition says, the *Banu Qurayza* negotiated with the attackers, breaking the agreement. After the siege lifted, the Muslims besieged them. They surrendered and accepted judgment by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a chief of the Aws, their former allies. He ruled that the men be executed and the women and children enslaved. The sira says this was carried out. The Qur'an refers to it in 33:26–27. Traditional numbers for those killed range from several hundred upward; historians note that the figures vary among the sources.

How to understand these events is debated. Muslim scholars have traditionally read them as punishment for broken treaties in wartime, under the customs of the day, not as acts against Jews as such; they point to the agreement of Medina and to Jewish communities that lived under Muslim rule for centuries after. Some historians question details of the Qurayza account. Others accept it. What can be said plainly is this: these were political and military conflicts between specific tribes in one town, and they should be described as such, not as a verdict on any religion.

words.d: the ditch dug to defend Medina in 627, which gave its name to the siege; Surah 33 refers to it
a Jewish tribe of Medina expelled in 624 after a dispute following Badr
a Jewish tribe of Medina expelled in 625; Surah 59 is read as referring to this
a Jewish tribe of Medina whose men were executed in 627 after the siege of the Trench, as the sira reports

look.title: Two Ways to Tell the Same Events
look.text: Reader A writes: 'The Jewish tribes of Medina broke their treaty, so they were punished.' Reader B writes: 'The Muslims expelled or killed the Jews of Medina.' Both sentences leave something out. Reader C writes: 'Three Jewish tribes of Medina, one after another, came into conflict with Muhammad's community over disputes and alliances during a war with Mecca; two were expelled and the men of the third were executed after a judgment by their former ally.'
look.prompt: What does each sentence leave out or assume? Which one would you want in a public-school textbook, and why?

check.q: What tactic saved Medina in 627, according to tradition?
choices: A trench dug across the open side of the town
check.why: Salman's suggestion of a trench stopped the cavalry of the allied tribes; hence 'the Battle of the Trench.'

check.q: Which Jewish tribe of Medina does tradition say negotiated with the attackers during the Trench?
check.why: The sira says the Banu Qurayza dealt with the besiegers; after the siege the men were executed by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's judgment.

check.q: How does this course describe the conflicts with the Jewish tribes of Medina?
choices: As proof that Islam is hostile to Judaism
As a myth with no basis
As political and military conflicts between specific tribes in one town
As events the Qur'an never mentions
check.why: The events are told factually as tribal conflicts in wartime; the Qur'an refers to them (33:26–27, Surah 59), and readers debate their meaning.

lessons.title: Hudaybiyyah and the Return to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: A truce with Mecca in 628 that seemed like a loss led, within two years, to the peaceful entry into Mecca in 630 and the clearing of the Kaaba.
reading: In 628, tradition says, Muhammad set out with about 1,400 followers to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, unarmed except for travelers' swords. Quraysh blocked them at a place called *Hudaybiyyah*, outside the city. After tense talks, the two sides signed a truce for ten years. The Muslims would go home this year and return for pilgrimage the next. The terms looked one-sided; some Muslims, the sira says, were angry. Yet Surah 48, Al-Fath ("Victory"), is read by commentators as coming on the road home from Hudaybiyyah, and it calls the treaty a clear victory.

Why a victory? Historians and Muslim scholars give the same answer. The truce meant Quraysh had treated Muhammad as an equal. It opened Arabia to Muslim preaching, and tribes joined in large numbers. Muslims did make the pilgrimage in 629. Then, in 630, a clash between tribes allied to each side broke the truce, and Muhammad marched on Mecca with a large force. The city surrendered almost without fighting. Tradition dates this to Ramadan, 8 AH, January 630.

The sira describes what happened next. Muhammad entered the Kaaba and had the idols removed and broken. He declared a general pardon for the people of Mecca, with a few named exceptions. He did not make Mecca his capital; he returned to Medina. Surah 110, An-Nasr ("Help" or "Succor"), is read by many as referring to this moment, when people entered the religion "in troops." Soon after, the Muslims fought and won a battle against other tribes at Hunayn, which the Qur'an names (9:25).

For Muslims, the return to Mecca completes a circle: the man driven out in 622 comes back in 630, and the house they believe Ibrahim built for one God is cleared for that one God. For historians, the years 628 to 630 are when a town's movement became the leading power in western Arabia. Both readings agree that the treaty, not the battles, was the turning point. The Qur'an itself makes that claim in Surah 48.

words.d: the place outside Mecca where a ten-year truce was signed in 628; Surah 48 calls it a victory
'Victory,' Surah 48, read as coming after the treaty of Hudaybiyyah
a battle in 630 soon after the return to Mecca, named in Qur'an 9:25

look.title: Fight Those Who Fight You
look.text: Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:190 (Surah Al-Baqarah), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Some reports place this verse around the time of Hudaybiyyah, when Muslims feared being attacked during pilgrimage. What limit does the verse set, and who is it addressed to?

check.q: What was agreed at Hudaybiyyah in 628?
choices: A ten-year truce between the Muslims and Quraysh
check.why: The truce let Muslims return for pilgrimage the next year and opened Arabia to Muslim preaching.

check.q: Which surah is read as calling the treaty of Hudaybiyyah a victory?
check.why: Al-Fath means 'Victory'; commentators say it came on the road home from Hudaybiyyah.

check.q: What does the sira say Muhammad did when he entered Mecca in 630?
choices: He cleared the Kaaba of idols and pardoned most of the city
check.why: Tradition describes a nearly bloodless entry, the removal of idols and a general pardon with few exceptions.

lessons.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and After
lessons.mainIdea: In 632 Muhammad made a final pilgrimage and gave a sermon on fairness and equality; he died in Medina that year, and the Qur'an was gathered into one book after him.
reading: In 632 (10 AH), tradition says, Muhammad led the pilgrimage to Mecca himself. Muslims call it the *Farewell Pilgrimage*. On the plain of Arafat he gave a sermon that is reported in the sira and hadith collections with varying wording. The reports have him say that all Muslims are brothers; that a person's life and property are sacred; that debts of blood from before Islam are cancelled; that men and women have rights over each other; and that no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor a white person than a black person, except by good conduct.

Commentators connect the pilgrimage to Qur'an 5:3, which says God has this day perfected the religion and completed his favor. Many Muslims hold it was among the last verses revealed. Another verse often read alongside the sermon is 49:13, which says God made humans into nations and tribes so they might know one another, and that the noblest is the most conscious of God. Muslim writers on race and equality, including African American Muslims in Chicago and elsewhere, have often turned to these two texts together.

A few months later, in June 632, tradition says Muhammad fell ill and died in Medina, in the room of his wife Aisha next to the mosque. He was buried there; his tomb is inside the Prophet's Mosque today. He had named no clear successor. Abu Bakr was chosen as the first *caliph*, or successor, by a group of leading Muslims. Shia Muslims hold that Muhammad had designated Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and that the choice of Abu Bakr set aside that wish. This disagreement is the root of the Sunni–Shia division, and both sides tell the story of 632 differently.

At his death, tradition says, the Qur'an existed as memorized recitation and as writings on leather, bone and palm stalks kept by various companions. After many reciters died in battle in 633, Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit collect the text. Under the third caliph, Uthman, around 650, an official copy was made and sent to the main cities. That is the story of the *mushaf*, the written Qur'an, as Muslim tradition tells it. Historians note that the early manuscripts, including the Birmingham folios, fit this picture of a text fixed within a generation.

words.d: Muhammad's last pilgrimage to Mecca in 632, where tradition says he gave a sermon on fairness and equality
'successor'; the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad, beginning with Abu Bakr
the written, bound Qur'an; tradition says Abu Bakr had it collected and Uthman had an official copy made c. 650

look.title: Nations and Tribes
look.text: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware.
look.cite: Qur'an 49:13 (Surah Al-Hujurat), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: According to this verse, why do different nations and tribes exist, and what makes a person noble? How does that match the reported words of the farewell sermon?

check.q: What did Muhammad reportedly say in the farewell sermon about Arabs and non-Arabs?
choices: No Arab is better than a non-Arab except by good conduct
Non-Arabs may not make the pilgrimage
check.why: The reported sermon denies any superiority by race or tribe; readers pair it with Qur'an 49:13.

check.q: What is the root of the Sunni–Shia division?
choices: Whether the Qur'an is in Arabic
Disagreement over who should have led after Muhammad's death
check.why: Sunnis accept Abu Bakr's selection as caliph; Shia hold Muhammad had designated Ali.

check.q: Under which caliph, according to tradition, was an official written Qur'an sent to the main cities?
check.why: Tradition says Uthman had the official mushaf copied and distributed c. 650, after Abu Bakr's earlier collection.

lessons.title: Why a Verse Came Down
lessons.mainIdea: Asbab al-nuzul are reports about the situation in which a verse was revealed; scholars collected them to help readers understand what a verse was answering.
reading: The Qur'an is not arranged in the order Muslims believe it was revealed, and most verses do not say what event they respond to. Early Muslims who had lived through the events remembered, and their reports were passed down. Scholars called these *asbab al-nuzul*, "the occasions of revelation" (one occasion is a sabab al-nuzul). A report typically says: such-and-such happened, and then this verse came down. The reports live in hadith collections and in *tafsir*, commentary on the Qur'an.

The best-known collection is by al-Wahidi, a scholar from Nishapur in Persia who died in 1075. His book, called simply Asbab al-Nuzul, gathers hundreds of reports arranged by surah. Al-Suyuti, an Egyptian scholar who died in 1505, made a stricter collection, keeping only reports he judged well attested. Al-Tabari, in his huge commentary (he died in 923), often gives several occasions for one verse and then says which he prefers.

A famous example is the opening of Surah 80, Abasa ("He Frowned"). The verses say that "he" frowned and turned away when a blind man came to him. Reports say a blind Muslim, Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, interrupted Muhammad while he was speaking with leaders of Quraysh, and that Muhammad frowned; then the verses came, rebuking him. Muslims read this as the Qur'an correcting the Prophet himself, and as a lesson that the poor and disabled matter as much as the powerful. Without the report, a reader might not know who frowned or why.

Scholars are careful with these reports. Several may exist for one verse and they may not agree. A report might be a guess by a later reader. And a famous rule in Islamic scholarship says that what counts is the general meaning of the words, not only the particular occasion. So the occasion helps, but it does not close the meaning. That is the tension the next lessons explore.

words.d: 'the occasions of revelation,' reports of the situations in which Qur'an verses were revealed
commentary that explains the Qur'an verse by verse
the scholar (died 1075) whose book Asbab al-Nuzul is the best-known collection of occasions of revelation

look.title: He Frowned
look.text: The surah opens by saying that he frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him, and asks how the speaker could know whether that man might grow in goodness or take heed. It contrasts him with the one who thinks himself independent, to whom the speaker attends.
look.cite: Qur'an 80:1–7 (Surah Abasa), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930; the occasion is reported in al-Wahidi's Asbab al-Nuzul (c. 1070)

lessons.title: One Verse, Two Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing the reported occasion of a verse such as 2:256 changes how readers weigh it, and readers still disagree about how far the occasion limits the meaning.
reading: Qur'an 2:256 begins, in Pickthall's words, "There is no compulsion in religion." It is one of the most quoted lines in the Qur'an. Reports of its occasion vary. One, going back to Ibn Abbas, says that before Islam some women of Medina who lost children had vowed to raise the next child as a Jew, so some Ansar families had Jewish sons. When the Banu Nadir were expelled, the fathers wanted to force these sons to become Muslims and stay, and the verse came to forbid it. Al-Tabari records this and similar reports.

With the occasion in mind, the verse reads as a specific ruling: parents may not force a grown child to change religion. Without it, the verse reads as a general principle: faith cannot be forced on anyone. Most Muslim scholars through history have taken it as a general principle, applying the rule that the general wording matters more than the particular case. Islamic law generally held that non-Muslims under Muslim rule were not to be forced to convert, and many jurists cite this verse.

But readers have also disagreed. Some medieval scholars argued the verse was later narrowed or replaced by verses commanding fighting, using a tool called *naskh*, abrogation, in which a later verse limits an earlier one. Others rejected that reading, and many modern Muslim scholars call 2:256 a foundation of religious freedom in Islam. The occasion of revelation is one piece of evidence each side uses, and they use it differently.

This is the point of studying asbab al-nuzul: not to settle the argument but to see how it is made. The same verse, the same report, and two careful readers can reach different conclusions about how wide the rule is. When you read any verse of the Qur'an, or any scripture, ask what it was answering and how far its readers have taken it. Both questions are part of understanding it.

words.d: abrogation; a tool in Islamic scholarship by which a later verse is held to limit or replace an earlier one
a rule in tafsir: the general wording of a verse counts, not only the particular occasion it answered
Muhammad's cousin (died c. 687), a source for many reports on the Qur'an's meaning and occasions

lessons.title: Verses on Fighting in Context
lessons.mainIdea: The Medinan verses on fighting each have reported occasions, and mainstream scholars read them with their context, limits and the verses around them.
reading: In Mecca the Muslims did not fight. In Medina, tradition says, permission came. Qur'an 22:39–40 is often named as the first verse to allow fighting; it says permission is given to those who are fought against because they were wronged and driven from their homes. Commentators tie it to the emigrants who lost everything in Mecca. Then 2:190–194 lays down rules: fight those who fight you, do not begin hostilities, fight in the sacred precinct only if attacked there, and stop if the other side stops.

Two verses in Surah 9, At-Tawbah, are the ones most argued about. Verse 9:5, sometimes called the "sword verse," tells the Muslims, after the sacred months, to fight the idolaters wherever they find them, but the next words say to let them go if they repent and pray. Verse 9:29 concerns fighting People of the Book who do not accept the rules of the community, until they pay the *jizya*, a tax. Commentators tie Surah 9 to 631, after the return to Mecca, when the Muslims broke off relations with tribes that had broken treaties. Verse 9:4 says treaties with those who kept them are to be honored.

Readers have handled these verses in more than one way. A minority of medieval jurists said 9:5 abrogated the gentler verses. Most classical scholars limited it to the Arab idolaters who had broken treaties, and read the Qur'an's whole set of war verses together: fight only those who fight you, keep treaties, do not exceed limits, and lean toward peace when the enemy does (8:61). Modern mainstream Muslim scholars overwhelmingly hold the second view, and most also say Islamic law forbids killing non-combatants. Extremist groups quote 9:5 alone; scholars answer by quoting the context.

For a student, the lesson is method. Read the verse before and the verse after. Ask the reported occasion. Ask who is being addressed and about whom. Ask how the tradition's own scholars, from al-Tabari to today, have read it. A verse on fighting in the Qur'an, like a verse on war in the Hebrew Bible, cannot be understood from a single line pulled out of its surah.

words.d: a name some give to Qur'an 9:5; scholars debate whether it is limited to the treaty-breaking tribes of 631
a tax that non-Muslims under Muslim rule paid in place of military service, named in 9:29
a person not taking part in fighting, such as a child or farmer; Islamic law generally forbids harming them

look.title: The Verse Before and the Verse After
look.text: Reader A quotes only the middle of 9:5: fight the idolaters wherever you find them. Reader B reads 9:4 first, which says to honor treaties with those who kept them, then 9:5 in full, including the words about letting those who repent go free, then 9:6, which says to give protection to any idolater who asks for it so he can hear the word of God, and then bring him to safety.
look.prompt: How does the meaning of 9:5 shift when 9:4 and 9:6 are read with it? Whom does each reader think the verse is about?

check.q: Which verses are often named as the first to permit fighting, according to commentators?
check.why: 22:39–40 gives permission to those who were wronged and driven out, which commentators tie to the emigrants.

check.q: How do most classical and modern Muslim scholars read 9:5?
choices: As the only verse on war that matters
As applying to all non-Muslims forever
As limited to the Arab tribes that broke treaties, read with the verses around it
check.why: Mainstream scholars limit the verse to its occasion in 631 and read it with 9:4, 9:6 and 2:190.

check.q: What does 2:190 forbid?
check.why: Pickthall: 'but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.'

lessons.title: Medinan Themes: Law, Family and the People of the Book
lessons.mainIdea: Medinan surahs are long and deal with law, family, community and the Qur'an's relationship to Jews and Christians, whom it calls People of the Book.
reading: The Medinan surahs look different from the Meccan ones. They are long. Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, has 286 verses; Surah 4, An-Nisa ("Women"), has 176. Their verses are longer too, and the rhyme is looser. They speak to a community that already believes and now needs rules. The Qur'an's longest single verse, 2:282, is about writing down a debt and having witnesses. Rules on fasting, pilgrimage, food, marriage, divorce, inheritance and charity are mostly Medinan.

Family law is a large part of this. Surah 4 sets shares of inheritance for daughters as well as sons (4:11), which historians note was new in Arabia, where women often inherited nothing. It also permits a man up to four wives on the condition of fairness (4:3), a verse commentators tie to the many widows and orphans left after Uhud. How these verses apply today is debated within Islam. Traditional jurists, reformers and Muslim feminists all read the same verses and reach different rules; that debate is a live part of the tradition, not something outside it.

The Medinan surahs also speak often of Jews and Christians. The Qur'an's term is *People of the Book*, those who received earlier scriptures. It says their God is the same God (29:46), that Muslims may eat their food and marry their women (5:5), and that those among them who believe and do good need not fear (2:62). It also argues with them, saying they altered or hid parts of their scriptures, and it criticizes specific groups sharply. Some verses are warm and some are hard, and often both appear in one surah.

Readers have sorted these verses in different ways. Some medieval scholars gave weight to the hard verses; many modern scholars and interfaith leaders stress the shared God and the earlier prophets. At the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, a convert named Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb presented Islam to an American audience alongside speakers from other faiths. The verses he could draw on, warm and hard, were the same ones readers weigh today.

words.d: a surah dated to after the hijra of 622; usually long and concerned with law and community
the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians, as peoples who received earlier scriptures
property passed on after a death; Surah 4 sets shares for daughters as well as sons
